title: A four-point failure of (J+, boxdot)-cubical excision
oneLine: A directed four-point closure space sends a nonzero integral relative one-cycle to zero, disproving interior-cover excision for normalized (J+, boxdot)-cubical homology.
abstract: This anonymous, unrefereed candidate gives a four-point interior cover in the inductive square of the directed interval J+ for which the integral relative cubical-homology map is not injective. In an explicit basis, the source has d1=[-1 -1] and d2=0, so H1(B,L) is Z; in the target, the identity square supplies the primitive column (1,-1), so H1(X,A)=0. The result is limited to normalized (J+, boxdot)-cubical singular homology and does not extend to categorical products, other intervals, symmetric graph closures, or other coefficient conventions. A written proof, complete Python and JavaScript stable-schema concordance, six semantic mutations, 15 tests, internal review, and hash-bound release gates support the candidate. Historical priority, independent reproduction, formal verification, specialist review, and peer review remain unestablished.
narration: Excision is a principle saying that, under the right cover, removing the same subspace from a space and a subspace should not change relative homology. This anonymous, unrefereed candidate gives a four-point failure for one precise cubical theory of closure spaces. Start with the directed interval J plus and form its inductive square. Let A contain the top and right points, and let B contain the bottom and left points. Their interiors cover all four points. The intersection L consists of two discrete points. Relative to L, B has two directed edges from zero zero. Their difference is a nonzero one-cycle, and an integer cocycle proves that it generates a copy of the integers. Relative to A, the same cycle becomes the boundary of the identity square. Thus the inclusion sends the nonzero group Z to the zero group, so the excision map is not injective. The claim is deliberately narrow: it concerns integral normalized cubical homology for the directed interval J plus with the inductive box product. It says nothing about the categorical product, the other interval objects, symmetric digital images, or other coefficient conventions. Python and JavaScript agree on the complete stable certificate, six convention mutations are rejected, and a fresh replay leaves all fifty-six package files unchanged. Those are producer-side checks, not independent validation, formal verification, specialist review, or peer review. Historical priority also remains unresolved. The scholarly creator is Anonymous. This synthetic-voice briefing is a communication aid, not additional mathematical evidence.

problem.name: AIM Problem 4.2: cubical homology and excision

keyResults: The sets A={10,01,11} and B={00,10,01} form an interior cover of X=J+ boxdot J+.
With integral coefficients, H1(B,L) is Z, generated by the difference of the two coordinate edges.
The identity square has relative boundary equal to that generator, so H1(X,A)=0.
The inclusion-induced map Z to 0 is not injective, and interior-cover excision fails for this named cubical theory.
The matrix certificate labels all four source and eight target degree-two columns; six semantic mutations are rejected in both encodings.
evidence: A seven-page canonical manuscript and aligned Markdown; explicit singleton closures and integer matrices; a complete stable JSON certificate; dependency-free Python and JavaScript encodings; 15 unit/audit tests; six semantic mutations; complete pre/post payload inventories; a 53-entry manifest over a 56-file package; bundled fast-gate and terminal receipts; source, novelty, licence, review and review-response records; a five-role producer-organised substantive review; one bounded confirmation that found a gate-plan portability P1, followed by explicit-bytecode deterministic repair and reseal; a clean public GitHub history; and exact GitHub/Zenodo asset readback. These establish public availability, integrity, producer replay and the stated finite computation—not historical priority, unaffiliated reproduction, formal verification, external specialist review, peer review, or impact.
